cites.quote: within 21 days after being served with the summons and complaint

stem: Park sues Delta Mills in federal court. Delta Mills is served with the summons and complaint on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. It does not waive service under Rule 4(d), no federal statute sets another time, and it has served no motion.
ask: By what date must Delta Mills serve its answer?

options.t: March 17, 2026
options.why: Counts 14 days, the period that Rule 12(a)(4)(A) applies only after a Rule 12 motion is denied. No motion was served here.

options.t: March 24, 2026
options.why: Correct. Service of the summons and complaint on March 3 starts the 21-day clock of Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(i); the 21st day is a Tuesday.

options.t: March 31, 2026
options.why: Counts 28 days, a period that appears nowhere in Rule 12(a)(1)(A).
Uses the 60-day period, which Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) gives only to a defendant that timely waived service under Rule 4(d).

explain: An answer is due 21 days after service of the summons and complaint (Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(i)). Counting from March 3 under Rule 6(a)(1), the 21st day is Tuesday, March 24, 2026. The 14-day and 60-day periods are triggered by a denied motion or a Rule 4(d) waiver, neither of which occurred.

cites.quote: within 60 days after the request for a waiver was sent

stem: Park mails Hale Foods, an Ohio company, a request to waive service under Rule 4(d). The request is sent to Hale Foods in Ohio on Monday, February 2, 2026. Hale Foods signs the waiver in time and returns it on Friday, February 20, 2026. No motion is served and no statute sets another time.
ask: By what date must Hale Foods serve its answer?

options.t: February 23, 2026
options.why: Counts 21 days from the request, ignoring the longer period that Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) gives a defendant that timely waives service.

options.t: April 21, 2026
options.why: Counts 60 days from the day the waiver was returned. Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) runs the period from when the request for a waiver was sent.

options.t: April 3, 2026
options.why: Correct. The waiver was timely, so Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) gives 60 days after the request was sent: February 2 plus 60 days is April 3.
Counts 90 days, which Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) allows only when the request was sent to a defendant outside any judicial district of the United States.

explain: A defendant that timely waived service must answer within 60 days after the request for a waiver was sent, or 90 days if it was sent outside the United States (Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii)). The request went to Ohio on February 2, so the 60-day period ends Friday, April 3, 2026. The date the waiver was returned does not start the clock.

cites.quote: if the court denies the motion or postpones its disposition until trial, the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after notice of the court's action

stem: Nash serves Ruiz Co. with a summons and complaint on Friday, May 1, 2026. On May 15 Ruiz Co. serves a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss. On Monday, June 8, 2026, the court denies the motion and notifies the parties that day. The court sets no different time for responding.
ask: By what date must Ruiz Co. serve its answer?

options.why: Treats the original 21-day period as unaffected. Under Rule 12(a)(4) serving a Rule 12 motion alters the period.
Counts 14 days from the day the motion was served. Rule 12(a)(4)(A) counts from notice of the court's action.
Counts 21 days after the denial. After a denied motion Rule 12(a)(4)(A) gives 14 days, not 21.
Correct. The court denied the motion on June 8, and Rule 12(a)(4)(A) requires the responsive pleading within 14 days after notice of that action.

explain: Serving a Rule 12 motion alters the answer period. If the court denies the motion, the responsive pleading is due within 14 days after notice of the denial (Rule 12(a)(4)(A)). Notice came Monday, June 8, so the answer is due Monday, June 22, 2026.

cites.quote: if the court grants a motion for a more definite statement, the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after the more definite statement is served

stem: Evans serves Frost Tech with the summons and complaint on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Frost Tech serves a Rule 12(e) motion for a more definite statement on September 10. The court grants it on Tuesday, September 22 and orders a cure. Evans serves the more definite statement on Thursday, October 1, 2026. The court sets no other time.
ask: By what date must Frost Tech serve its answer?

options.t: October 15, 2026
options.why: Correct. Because the court granted a Rule 12(e) motion, Rule 12(a)(4)(B) gives 14 days after the more definite statement is served, October 1.

options.t: October 6, 2026
options.why: Counts 14 days from the order granting the motion. Rule 12(a)(4)(B) runs from service of the more definite statement.

options.t: October 22, 2026
options.why: Counts 21 days after the more definite statement. Rule 12(a)(4)(B) fixes 14 days, not the 21 days of Rule 12(a)(1).

options.t: September 22, 2026
options.why: Keeps the original 21-day deadline as if the Rule 12(e) motion had not altered the period. Rule 12(a)(4) says it does.

explain: A Rule 12(e) motion is a motion under Rule 12, so it alters the answer period. When the court grants it, the responsive pleading is due 14 days after the more definite statement is served (Rule 12(a)(4)(B)). Service on October 1 makes the deadline Thursday, October 15, 2026.

cites.quote: A party must serve an answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim within 21 days after being served with the pleading that states the counterclaim or crossclaim.
3 days are added after the period would otherwise expire under Rule 6(a)

stem: Park sues Lin Corp. Lin Corp. answers and asserts a counterclaim against Park. Lin Corp. serves the counterclaim on Park's lawyer by mail under Rule 5(b)(2)(C) on Monday, April 6, 2026. Park's time to respond is not changed by any order or motion.
ask: By what date must Park serve its answer to the counterclaim?

options.t: April 20, 2026
options.why: Counts 14 days. That period applies only after a motion is denied or a more definite statement is served under Rule 12(a)(4), not to a counterclaim.

options.t: April 27, 2026
options.why: Counts the 21 days of Rule 12(a)(1)(B) but forgets that Rule 6(d) adds 3 days after service by mail.

options.t: April 30, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(a)(1)(B) gives 21 days (April 27), and Rule 6(d) adds 3 days after the period expires because service was by mail.
Counts 28 days, a period that Rule 12(a)(1)(B) does not contain.

explain: An answer to a counterclaim is due 21 days after service of the counterclaim (Rule 12(a)(1)(B)): Monday, April 27. Service by mail under Rule 5(b)(2)(C) adds 3 days after the period would otherwise expire (Rule 6(d)), so the deadline is Thursday, April 30, 2026.

cites.quote: But a party may assert the following defenses by motion
failure to join a party under Rule 19

stem: Cho Bank is sued for breach of a loan contract and has not yet answered. Cho Bank's only objection is that Gray, whom Rule 19 would require to be joined, was not made a party.
ask: May Cho Bank raise this objection by a motion made before it answers?

options.t: No, every defense must be asserted in the answer and none may be raised by pre-answer motion.
options.why: Reads only the first sentence of Rule 12(b). The next sentence lets a party assert listed defenses by motion.

options.t: No, only the defenses in Rule 12(b)(1) through (6) may be raised by motion.
options.why: Adds a limit the rule does not have. Rule 12(b)(7) lists failure to join a party under Rule 19.

options.t: No, it may be raised only by a motion for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close.
options.why: Confuses Rule 12(c) with Rule 12(b). A Rule 12(b) motion must be made before pleading if a responsive pleading is allowed.

options.t: Yes; Rule 12(b)(7) lists this defense, and a motion must come before pleading.
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(b)(7) allows the defense by motion, made before pleading.

explain: Rule 12(b) lets a party assert seven listed defenses by motion, including failure to join a party under Rule 19 (12(b)(7)). A motion asserting any of them must be made before pleading when a responsive pleading is allowed, so Cho Bank may move now.

cites.quote: a party that makes a motion under this rule must not make another motion under this rule raising a defense or objection that was available to the party but omitted from its earlier motion
omitting it from a motion in the circumstances described in Rule 12(g)(2)

stem: Evans sues Frost Tech, an out-of-state firm, in federal court. Before answering, Frost Tech serves a Rule 12(b)(6) motion and says nothing about personal jurisdiction, though it could have. The court denies the motion. Frost Tech then serves a second Rule 12 motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, before filing any answer.
ask: What is the result of the second motion?

options.t: It must be heard, because no answer has been served and a Rule 12(b) motion is timely before pleading.
options.why: Ignores the limit in Rule 12(g)(2) on a further Rule 12 motion raising a defense that was available but omitted.

options.t: It is barred, but Frost Tech may plead lack of personal jurisdiction in its answer.
options.why: Rule 12(h)(1)(A) waives the defense when omitted in the Rule 12(g)(2) circumstances, so it cannot be revived in the answer.

options.t: It is barred: the defense was available but omitted from the first motion, so it is waived.
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(g)(2) bars the second motion, and Rule 12(h)(1)(A) waives a Rule 12(b)(2) defense omitted that way.

options.t: It must be heard, because Rule 12(b) says no defense is waived by joining it with other defenses in a motion.
options.why: Misreads Rule 12(b)'s last sentence. Joining defenses never waives them; omitting a defense from the motion does.

explain: Personal jurisdiction was available when Frost Tech made its first Rule 12 motion but was omitted. Rule 12(g)(2) bars a second Rule 12 motion on it, and Rule 12(h)(1)(A) waives a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense so omitted. The defense is gone, in a motion or in the answer.

cites.quote: Except as provided in Rule 12(h)(2) or (3)
Failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, to join a person required by Rule 19(b), or to state a legal defense to a claim may be raised
by a motion under Rule 12(c)

stem: Gill sues Hart Co. Hart Co. serves a pre-answer motion under Rule 12(b)(2) only, and the court denies it. Hart Co. answers, and the pleadings close. Hart Co. then moves under Rule 12(c) for judgment on the pleadings, arguing the complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. Gill responds that Hart Co. already made its one Rule 12 motion.
ask: Is Hart Co.'s Rule 12(c) motion barred?

options.t: No; Rule 12(g)(2) yields to Rule 12(h)(2), which allows this defense by a Rule 12(c) motion.
options.why: Correct. The Rule 12(g)(2) bar is subject to Rule 12(h)(2), and 12(h)(2)(B) preserves this defense for a Rule 12(c) motion.

options.t: Yes. Rule 12(g)(2) allows one Rule 12 motion per party, whatever defense it raises.
options.why: Overlooks the opening exception in Rule 12(g)(2) for what Rule 12(h)(2) or (3) provides.

options.t: Yes. Failure to state a claim is waived under Rule 12(h)(1) when omitted from the first motion.
options.why: Rule 12(h)(1) waives only defenses in Rule 12(b)(2)-(5). Failure to state a claim is governed by Rule 12(h)(2).

options.t: No, but only if the court first grants Hart Co. leave under Rule 15.
options.why: Invents a leave requirement. Rule 12(h)(2)(B) preserves the defense for a Rule 12(c) motion without leave.

explain: Rule 12(g)(2) bars successive Rule 12 motions, except as Rule 12(h)(2) or (3) provide. Rule 12(h)(2) preserves failure to state a claim and allows it to be raised by a Rule 12(c) motion. Hart Co.'s earlier Rule 12(b)(2) motion therefore does not bar this one.

cites.quote: If the court determines at any time that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, the court must dismiss the action.

stem: Alder sues Birch Co. After 14 months of discovery and a pending summary judgment motion, the court determines that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction. Birch Co. never raised lack of subject-matter jurisdiction in a motion or in its answer. Alder argues that Birch Co. waived the point.
ask: What must the court do?

options.t: Proceed, because a Rule 12(b) defense not raised in the answer or a pre-answer motion is waived.
options.why: Treats every Rule 12(b) defense as waivable. Rule 12(h)(1) waives only Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defenses.

options.t: Proceed, because Birch Co. participated in discovery and summary judgment practice.
options.why: Rule 12(h)(3) has no participation exception. The court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks jurisdiction.

options.t: Dismiss only if Birch Co. moves before trial, because Rule 12(i) requires a defense to be heard then.
options.why: Rule 12(h)(3) puts the duty on the court. It does not wait for a motion.

options.t: Dismiss the action, because the court must do so if it determines at any time that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction.
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(h)(3) applies at any time, without regard to waiver.

explain: Rule 12(h)(1) waives only defenses in Rule 12(b)(2)-(5). Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction is not waived, and under Rule 12(h)(3) the court must dismiss if it determines at any time that it lacks jurisdiction.

cites.quote: failing to either: (i) make it by motion under this rule; or (ii) include it in a responsive pleading or in an amendment allowed by Rule 15(a)(1) as a matter of course
21 days after serving it

stem: Ivy sues Jet Co. Jet Co. makes no Rule 12 motion and serves its answer on Monday, March 2, 2026, which omits any objection to venue. On Friday, March 20, 2026, Jet Co. serves its first amended answer adding the defense of improper venue. Ivy moves to strike that defense as waived.
ask: Is the improper-venue defense waived?

options.t: No. It was included in an amendment allowed as a matter of course, which Rule 12(h)(1)(B)(ii) accepts.
options.why: Correct. The answer was amended once within 21 days of service (Rule 15(a)(1)(A)), and Rule 12(h)(1)(B)(ii) counts that amendment.

options.t: Yes. A defense omitted from the original answer is waived, and amendment cannot revive it.
options.why: Ignores that Rule 12(h)(1)(B)(ii) expressly counts an amendment allowed by Rule 15(a)(1) as a matter of course.

options.t: No, but only if the court grants leave under Rule 15(a)(2).
options.why: Adds a leave requirement. March 20 is within 21 days of serving the answer, so no leave is needed.

options.t: No. Improper venue may be raised at any time before trial under Rule 12(i).
options.why: Rule 12(i) governs when a raised defense is heard, not whether it was preserved.

explain: Improper venue is a Rule 12(b)(3) defense, waived by failing to raise it in a motion or in a responsive pleading or an amendment allowed by Rule 15(a)(1) as a matter of course (Rule 12(h)(1)(B)). March 20 is 18 days after service, so the amendment was as of right and preserved the defense.

cites.quote: so vague or ambiguous that the party cannot reasonably prepare a response

stem: Kemp sues Lowe. The complaint says only that Lowe "breached one or more of the parties' agreements, causing loss." Lowe has two agreements with Kemp and cannot reasonably prepare a response. Lowe has not answered and wants to challenge the complaint without yet asking for dismissal.
ask: Which motion fits Lowe's problem most directly?

options.t: Motion to strike under Rule 12(f)
options.why: Rule 12(f) targets an insufficient defense or redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter. Nothing here is of that kind.

options.t: Motion for a more definite statement under Rule 12(e)
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(e) applies when a pleading is so vague or ambiguous that the party cannot reasonably prepare a response.

options.t: Motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)
options.why: Seeks dismissal for failure to state a claim. Lowe's complaint is that the pleading is unintelligible, which is the Rule 12(e) problem.

options.t: Motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c)
options.why: Premature: Rule 12(c) is available only after the pleadings are closed, and Lowe has not answered.

explain: Rule 12(e) lets a party move for a more definite statement of a pleading to which a response is allowed but which is so vague or ambiguous that it cannot reasonably prepare a response. The motion must be made before answering and must point out the defects and details desired.

cites.quote: After the pleadings are closed—but early enough not to delay trial—a party may move for judgment on the pleadings.
by a motion under Rule 12(c)

stem: Nash sues Mora Co. Mora Co. answers on May 4 without any Rule 12 motion. There are no counterclaims, and the pleadings are now closed. Trial is not set for a year. Mora Co. concludes the complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.
ask: How may Mora Co. now present that defense by motion?

options.t: By a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, which may be made at any time before trial.
options.why: Rule 12(b) requires a motion asserting a listed defense to be made before pleading. Mora Co. has already answered.

options.t: It cannot; failure to state a claim is waived once the answer is served without it.
options.why: Rule 12(h)(2) preserves this defense. Only the Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defenses are waived under Rule 12(h)(1).

options.t: It may be raised only at trial under Rule 12(h)(2)(C).
options.why: Rule 12(h)(2) lists trial as one option, but Rule 12(h)(2)(B) also permits a Rule 12(c) motion now.

options.t: By a Rule 12(c) motion for judgment on the pleadings, which Rule 12(h)(2)(B) allows.
options.why: Correct. The pleadings are closed, so Rule 12(c) is available, and Rule 12(h)(2)(B) preserves this defense for that motion.

explain: A Rule 12(b) motion must come before pleading, but failure to state a claim is preserved by Rule 12(h)(2): it may be raised in a pleading, by a Rule 12(c) motion, or at trial. With the pleadings closed, Mora Co. may move for judgment on the pleadings.

cites.quote: If, on a motion under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56.

stem: Nash sues Orr Co. for breach of contract. Orr Co. serves a Rule 12(b)(6) motion and attaches a sworn affidavit from its chief financial officer and bank records showing payment. The court considers the affidavit and records and does not exclude them.
ask: What must happen to the motion?

options.t: It stays a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, and the court may rely on the affidavit without notice to Nash.
options.why: Rule 12(d) provides otherwise: with outside matters not excluded, the motion is treated as one for summary judgment.

options.t: It is treated as a Rule 56 motion, and all parties must get a reasonable opportunity to present material.
options.why: Correct. Rule 12(d) converts the motion and requires that opportunity.

options.t: It is automatically denied, and Orr Co. must then serve its answer within 14 days after the denial.
options.why: Rule 12(d) converts the motion rather than denying it; the 14-day period of Rule 12(a)(4)(A) is not triggered by conversion.

options.t: It is treated as a Rule 12(c) motion, which allows outside matters to be considered without conversion.
options.why: Rule 12(d) applies to Rule 12(c) motions too, and Rule 12(c) has no exception for outside matters.

explain: When matters outside the pleadings are presented on a Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion and the court does not exclude them, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56, and all parties must get a reasonable opportunity to present pertinent material (Rule 12(d)).

cites.quote: After the pleadings are closed
matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court
If a party so moves, any defense listed in Rule 12(b)(1)-(7)

stem: Zed sues Quo Co. The pleadings close in March. In April, Quo Co. moves for judgment on the pleadings and attaches a sworn declaration from its operations manager on a disputed fact. The court does not exclude the declaration. Quo Co.'s answer also asserted failure to join a party under Rule 19, and Quo Co. asks that this defense be heard and decided before trial. Zed has served no other motion, and no one disputes subject-matter jurisdiction.
ask: Which Rule 12 provisions are triggered by these facts?

options.t: Rule 12(c)
options.why: Triggered: the pleadings are closed and Quo Co. moves for judgment on the pleadings.

options.t: Rule 12(d)
options.why: Triggered: matters outside the pleadings were presented and not excluded, so the motion is treated as one for summary judgment.

options.t: Rule 12(i)
options.why: Triggered: a party moved that a listed Rule 12(b) defense be heard, so it must be heard and decided before trial unless deferred.

options.t: Rule 12(e)
options.why: Not triggered: no pleading is claimed to be too vague to answer.

options.t: Rule 12(f)(2)
options.why: Not triggered: no one moves to strike matter from a pleading.

options.t: Rule 12(h)(3)
options.why: Not triggered: no one raises a question of subject-matter jurisdiction.

explain: The closed pleadings make Rule 12(c) available. Presenting an unexcluded declaration converts the motion to summary judgment (Rule 12(d)). Quo Co.'s motion that its Rule 12(b)(7) defense be heard triggers Rule 12(i), which requires a decision before trial unless the court defers it.

cites.quote: 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or 21 days after service of a motion under Rule 12(b), (e), or (f), whichever is earlier

stem: Park serves her complaint on Delta Mills on Monday, March 2, 2026. On Monday, March 16, 2026, Delta Mills serves a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss and no answer. Park has not amended before and has no written consent or court order allowing amendment.
ask: What is the last day on which Park may amend her complaint once as a matter of course?

options.t: March 23, 2026
options.why: Counts only 21 days after serving the complaint. A complaint requires a responsive pleading, so Rule 15(a)(1)(B) also applies and runs from the Rule 12(b) motion.

options.t: March 30, 2026
options.why: Counts 14 days after the motion. Rule 15(a)(1)(B) allows 21 days after service of the Rule 12(b) motion, not 14.

options.t: April 6, 2026
options.why: Correct. The complaint requires a responsive pleading, so Rule 15(a)(1)(B) allows 21 days after service of the Rule 12(b) motion (March 16), ending April 6.

options.t: April 13, 2026
options.why: Counts 28 days after the motion, a period that Rule 15(a)(1) does not contain.

explain: A pleading that requires a responsive pleading may be amended once as a matter of course within 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or of a Rule 12(b), (e), or (f) motion, whichever is earlier (Rule 15(a)(1)(B)). The motion was served March 16, so the last day is Monday, April 6, 2026.

cites.quote: 21 days after serving it
only with the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave

stem: Blake sues Ames. Ames serves an answer on Monday, March 2, 2026, which requires no responsive pleading. On Monday, April 6, 2026, Ames serves an amended answer, its first, adding an affirmative defense. Blake has not consented in writing, and the court has not granted leave. Blake moves to strike the amended answer.
ask: Is Ames's amended answer proper?

options.t: Yes, because Ames amended within 21 days after service of a responsive pleading under Rule 15(a)(1)(B).
options.why: An answer is a pleading to which no responsive pleading is required, so Rule 15(a)(1)(B) does not apply to it.

options.t: Yes, because a party may amend at any time before trial without leave.
options.why: Describes no rule. Outside the 21-day window of Rule 15(a)(1), Rule 15(a)(2) requires written consent or leave.

options.t: No, because a party may never amend an answer without a court order.
options.why: Overstates the rule. Rule 15(a)(1)(A) lets a party amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after serving the pleading.

options.t: No, because it came 35 days after service, outside Rule 15(a)(1)(A), and neither written consent nor leave exists.
options.why: Correct. Beyond the 21-day window Rule 15(a)(2) permits amendment only with the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave.

explain: An answer requires no responsive pleading, so the only as-of-right period is 21 days after serving it (Rule 15(a)(1)(A)). The amended answer was served 35 days later, so Ames needed Blake's written consent or the court's leave (Rule 15(a)(2)). It had neither.

cites.quote: A party may amend its pleading once as a matter of course
only with the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave

stem: Cole sues Dunn. Cole has already amended her complaint once as a matter of course. Forty days later Cole's lawyer phones Dunn's lawyer, who says orally, "Fine by me." Cole then serves a second amended complaint with no motion for leave and no written consent. Dunn moves to strike it.
ask: How should the court rule on Dunn's motion?

options.t: Deny it, because oral consent from opposing counsel satisfies Rule 15(a)(2).
options.why: Rule 15(a)(2) calls for the opposing party's written consent. An oral "fine by me" is not that.

options.t: Grant it, because Cole has no written consent and no leave, and her one amendment as a matter of course is used up.
options.why: Correct. Rule 15(a)(1) allows an amendment as a matter of course once; Rule 15(a)(2) requires written consent or leave for any other.

options.t: Deny it, because a second amendment is allowed as a matter of course within 14 days under Rule 15(a)(3).
options.why: Rule 15(a)(3) governs the time to respond to an amended pleading, not a right to amend again.

options.t: Grant it, because a plaintiff may never amend a complaint more than once.
options.why: Overstates the rule. A further amendment is allowed with written consent or the court's leave, which the court should freely give when justice so requires.

explain: Rule 15(a)(1) permits one amendment as a matter of course. Every other amendment needs the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave (Rule 15(a)(2)). Cole already used her one amendment, and oral consent is not written consent, so the amended complaint is improper without leave.

cites.quote: When an issue not raised by the pleadings is tried by the parties' express or implied consent, it must be treated in all respects as if raised in the pleadings.
But failure to amend does not affect the result of the trial of that issue.

stem: Grant sues Hill for breach of a written contract. At a bench trial both sides present evidence, without objection from either, that the parties orally modified the contract. Neither pleaded modification, and no one moved to amend. The court finds for Grant on the modification issue. Hill moves to vacate, arguing the court decided an issue no pleading raised.
ask: How should the court rule on Hill's motion?

options.t: Grant it, because a judgment may rest only on issues raised in the pleadings.
options.why: Rule 15(b)(2) treats an issue tried by consent as if raised in the pleadings.

options.t: Grant it, unless Grant moved to amend before the trial ended.
options.why: Rule 15(b)(2) says failure to amend does not affect the result of the trial of that issue, and a party may move even after judgment.

options.t: Deny it; the issue was tried by implied consent, and failure to amend does not affect the result.
options.why: Correct. Rule 15(b)(2) treats it as if pleaded and says failure to amend does not affect the result.

options.t: Deny it, but only if the court first grants Hill a continuance under Rule 15(b)(1).
options.why: Rule 15(b)(1) concerns an objection at trial. Hill did not object, so Rule 15(b)(2) applies.

explain: An issue tried by the parties' express or implied consent must be treated in all respects as if raised in the pleadings, and failure to amend does not affect the result (Rule 15(b)(2)). Both sides litigated modification without objection, so the judgment stands.

cites.quote: the amendment asserts a claim or defense that arose out of the conduct, transaction, or occurrence set out—or attempted to be set out—in the original pleading

stem: Quinn is injured in a collision with Reed's truck. Quinn timely sues Reed for negligent driving. After the limitation period expires, Quinn amends to add a claim against Reed for negligent maintenance of the same truck, arising from the same collision. Nothing in the law that supplies the limitation period mentions relation back. Reed moves to dismiss the added claim as untimely.
ask: Which provision most directly lets the added claim relate back?

options.t: Rule 15(c)(1)(A)
options.why: Applies only when the law providing the limitation period allows relation back. The stem says it does not address the subject.

options.t: Rule 15(c)(1)(C)
options.why: Governs amendments that change the party or the naming of the party. Quinn is adding a claim against the same defendant.

options.t: Rule 15(d)
options.why: Concerns supplemental pleadings about events after the pleading date. The collision occurred before the original complaint.

options.t: Rule 15(c)(1)(B)
options.why: Correct. The added claim arose out of the same occurrence, the collision, set out in the original pleading.

explain: An amendment relates back when it asserts a claim that arose out of the conduct, transaction, or occurrence set out in the original pleading (Rule 15(c)(1)(B)). The maintenance claim arises from the same collision. Rule 15(c)(1)(A) does not help because the limitation law is silent, and Rule 15(c)(1)(C) concerns changes of party.

cites.quote: within the period provided by Rule 4(m) for serving the summons and complaint
If a defendant is not served within 90 days after the complaint is filed

stem: On Tuesday, January 6, 2026, Park files suit against "Delta Mills Inc.," mistaking it for Delta Mills LLC, the related entity that runs the plant and shares its manager and address. The limitation period expires May 20, 2026, and the law supplying it does not allow relation back. On June 8, 2026, Park serves an amended complaint naming the LLC. The claim arises from the same occurrence.
ask: For the amendment to relate back under Rule 15(c)(1)(C), by what date must the LLC have received notice of the action?

options.t: January 27, 2026

cites.quote: the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after notice of the court's action
must not make another motion under this rule
omitting it from a motion in the circumstances described in Rule 12(g)(2)

stem: Vega serves Wolf Corp. with a summons and complaint on Monday, June 1, 2026. On June 15, Wolf Corp. serves a motion under Rule 12(b)(6) that does not mention venue, though venue was objectionable and the point was available. The court denies the motion on Monday, July 6, and notifies the parties that day. On July 20, Wolf Corp. serves its answer, which asserts that venue is improper. Vega moves to strike the venue defense.
ask: Which rules decide whether the answer was timely and whether the venue defense survives?

options.t: Rule 12(a)(4)(A)
options.why: Triggered: the motion was denied July 6, so the answer was due 14 days later, July 20.

options.t: Rule 12(g)(2)
options.why: Triggered: the venue defense was available but omitted from Wolf Corp.'s earlier Rule 12 motion.

options.t: Rule 12(h)(1)(A)
options.why: Triggered: omitting a Rule 12(b)(3) defense from a motion in the circumstances of Rule 12(g)(2) waives it.

options.t: Rule 12(h)(2)
options.why: Not triggered: it preserves failure to state a claim and similar defenses, not improper venue.

options.t: Rule 12(h)(3)
options.why: Not triggered: no one contends the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction.

options.t: Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii)
options.why: Not triggered: Wolf Corp. was served with the summons and did not waive service under Rule 4(d).

explain: The denial on July 6 made the answer due July 20 (Rule 12(a)(4)(A)), so it was timely. But venue was available and omitted from the earlier Rule 12 motion (Rule 12(g)(2)), which waives a Rule 12(b)(3) defense under Rule 12(h)(1)(A).

The court may strike from a pleading an insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter.
A motion under this rule may be joined with any other motion allowed by this rule.

stem: Xu sues Yard Co. in a single complaint. Paragraph 9 contains insulting, irrelevant remarks about the family of Yard Co.'s owner. Paragraph 12 refers to "the contract," though Yard Co. has two contracts with Xu, and Yard Co. cannot reasonably prepare a response to it. Yard Co. also believes the complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. Yard Co. has not answered, Xu has served no other pleading, and Yard Co. plans to file all of its motions together in a single paper.
ask: Which rules support the combined motion Yard Co. may make before answering?

options.t: Rule 12(e)
options.why: Triggered: Paragraph 12 is so vague that Yard Co. cannot reasonably prepare a response.

options.t: Rule 12(f)
options.why: Triggered: Paragraph 9 is immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter, and Yard Co. has not yet responded.

options.t: Rule 12(b)(6)
options.why: Triggered: Yard Co. may assert failure to state a claim by motion before pleading.

options.t: Rule 12(c)
options.why: Not triggered: no pleadings are closed because Yard Co. has not answered.

options.t: Rule 12(d)
options.why: Not triggered: no matters outside the pleadings have been presented.

options.t: Rule 12(g)(1)
options.why: Triggered: Yard Co. plans to join these motions, and a Rule 12 motion may be joined with any other motion allowed by Rule 12.

explain: A vague paragraph supports a Rule 12(e) motion, a scandalous paragraph a Rule 12(f) motion, and failure to state a claim a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. Rule 12(g)(1) lets Yard Co. join them. Rule 12(c) needs closed pleadings and Rule 12(d) needs outside matters, and neither exists here.

cites.quote: within the time remaining to respond to the original pleading or within 14 days after service of the amended pleading, whichever is later

stem: Park serves her complaint on Gale Co. on Monday, March 2, 2026, so Gale Co.'s answer would be due March 23. On Friday, March 20, Park hand-delivers to Gale Co. an amended complaint, which she may file as a matter of course. Gale Co. has served no answer or motion, and the court has not ordered any time for responding.
ask: By what date must Gale Co. serve its response to the amended complaint?

options.t: April 3, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 15(a)(3) gives the later of the time remaining on the original (March 23) or 14 days after service of the amended pleading (April 3).

options.t: March 23, 2026
options.why: Uses the time remaining on the original complaint and ignores the 14-day alternative, which is later and so controls under Rule 15(a)(3).

options.t: April 6, 2026
options.why: Counts 14 days from the original March 23 deadline. Rule 15(a)(3) counts 14 days from service of the amended pleading.

options.t: April 10, 2026
options.why: Counts 21 days from the amended complaint. Rule 15(a)(3) fixes 14 days, not the 21 days of Rule 12(a).

explain: Rule 15(a)(3) requires a response to an amended pleading within the time remaining to respond to the original or 14 days after service of the amended pleading, whichever is later. The original period ran to March 23. Fourteen days after March 20 is Friday, April 3, which is later and controls.

cites.quote: the judge must issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60 days after any defendant has appeared

stem: Park sues two defendants. The first defendant is served with the complaint on Tuesday, January 6, 2026, and appears on Monday, February 9, 2026. The second defendant is served on Tuesday, February 3, 2026, and appears on Friday, February 27, 2026. The judge finds no good cause for delay and has received the parties' Rule 26(f) report.
ask: By what date must the judge issue the scheduling order?

options.t: April 10, 2026
options.why: Counts 60 days from the appearance. Rule 16(b)(2) requires the earlier of that date and the 90-day date, and April 6 is earlier.

options.t: March 9, 2026
options.why: Counts 60 days from service. The 60-day period in Rule 16(b)(2) runs from an appearance, and the 90-day period runs from service.

options.t: April 6, 2026
options.why: Correct. Ninety days after service (January 6) is April 6, and it is earlier than 60 days after the appearance (April 10).
Counts 90 days from the appearance. The 90-day period in Rule 16(b)(2) runs from service of the complaint.

explain: Absent good cause for delay, the scheduling order must issue within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served or 60 days after any defendant has appeared (Rule 16(b)(2)). Ninety days after the first service, January 6, is April 6; sixty days after the first appearance, February 9, is April 10. The second defendant's dates are later. The earlier, April 6, controls.
